sources.news_title: Navy and Marine Corps Review Boards Reject Pentagon Orders to Discharge Transgender Service Members
U.S. military boards go rogue to defy Pete Hegseth’s ban on transgender troops * WorldNetDaily * by Jillian Butler, Daily Caller News Foundation
sources.text:
Military boards are disobeying Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ban on openly transgender-identifying service members in the U.S. Armed Forces.
Nine of 12 Navy and Marine Corps review boards have recommended retaining transgender service members despite Pentagon directives calling for their discharge, according to The New York Times. The decisions raise questions about enforcement of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s military personnel policies and whether individual review boards are prioritizing their own ideology over the Pentagon’s stated readiness standards.
Directly after this executive order, the Pentagon enacted a system paying transgender service members to voluntarily separate from the military, the Times reported. As a result, hundreds left.
Navy & Marine Corps review boards are defying Pentagon policy on transgender troops, recommending that 9 of 12 service members reviewed be retained rather than discharged from the military.
The recommendations are not final, and civilian Navy leadership can still overturn them. https://t.co/rbIMNmZ0Tx
— Real America’s Voice (RAV) (@RealAmVoice) October 24, 2026
Those who challenged their dismissal faced three-member separation boards, according to the outlet. Those officers were given a set of criteria that a service member must meet to be dismissed. Boards of sailors and Marines have completely disregarded the criteria.
The Pentagon told the Daily Caller News Foundation that it does not comment on ongoing litigation.
“The Armed Forces have been afflicted with radical gender ideology to appease activists unconcerned with the requirements of military service like physical and mental health, selflessness, and unit cohesion,” President Donald Trump Stated in a January 2025 Executive Order.
“[E]xpressing a false ‘gender identity’ divergent from an individual’s sex cannot satisfy the rigorous standards necessary for military service … adoption of a gender identity inconsistent with an individual’s sex conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle, even in one’s personal life. A man’s assertion that he is a woman, and his requirement that others honor this falsehood, is not consistent with the humility and selflessness required of a service member.”
Marine Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras, a biological female, was put on paid leave in April due to a 2017 sex change hormone usage and her choice to identify as a male, according to the Times. In August, she was flown from Hawaii to Marine Corps Base Quantico to face a separation board. At the hearing, a government lawyer presented documents proving her struggles with gender identity. Rather than circle “a history of cross sex hormone therapy,” automatic grounds for separation, they circled “remains qualified.”
The Navy has nearly twice as many people who identify as gay, bisexual or transgender compared to other branches which indicated potential ideological bias, the Times reported.

sources.news_title: Navy, Marine Boards Vote to Keep Transgender Troops Despite Hegseth Ban
sources.text:
Navy, Marine Boards Vote to Keep Transgender Troops Despite Hegseth Ban
Navy and Marine Corps review boards set up to discharge transgender service members under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ban have instead voted to keep them in most cases.
The boards voted to retain transgender members in nine of 12 cases, according to a New York Times report by Dave Philipps. The Pentagon keeps the proceedings secret, and the Times compiled the figures from service members and lawyers.
In the Navy, which began hearings in July, nine boards produced seven votes to retain. In the Marine Corps, which started in August, three boards produced two votes to keep the member.
In the third Marine case, the board voted to discharge but wrote that its members unanimously believed the Marine should “be retained based on his commendable service record and unique skills.”
The pattern does not extend to the other branches. The Army has held about 50 hearings and voted to discharge in all but about five, while the Air Force has discharged in roughly six known cases.
Recommendations, Not Final Word
The decisions are only recommendations. Politically appointed service secretaries can reverse them, and pending legal challenges could pause or end the ban. The services and the Defense Department declined to comment, citing litigation.
The three-member boards are drawn from rank-and-file officers and enlisted personnel. Under the rules, any evidence of being transgender requires dismissal, and members may not weigh performance, critical skills or combat records.
Members receive a one-page findings sheet and are instructed to circle wording that the service member is not qualified to serve, the Times reported.
Marine Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras, a supply and logistics specialist with three overseas deployments, was flown from Hawaii to Quantico in August. His board crossed out language on the sheet and circled “remains qualified.”
“You have war fighters looking at war fighters,” Contreras told the Times. “They see I’ve always done my job, I’ve deployed, I’ve mentored other Marines, followed the rules.”
His lawyer, Priya Rashid, said she cannot explain the shift. “I’m worried that if the pattern becomes too apparent, the government will just change the processes and procedures again so that the pattern can be extinguished,” she said.
Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force lawyer who teaches at Southwestern Law School, said the boards are refusing “to rubber-stamp a nonchoice given to them by the administration.”
The administration argues transgender troops, about 4,250 people or roughly 0.1% of the force, burden military effectiveness. Trump’s January 2025 executive order said service “must be reserved for those mentally and physically fit for duty.”
The report drew fire on the right. The Daily Caller News Foundation framed the votes as military leaders disobeying Hegseth’s ban, and Philipps discussed his findings on CNN, Mediaite reported.
The Pentagon earlier offered transgender troops payments to leave voluntarily, and hundreds did. Those who stayed to contest dismissal have waited in limbo, some for more than a year.

Military Boards Are Quietly Defying Hegseth’s Transgender Ban Orders by Voting to Keep Gender-Confused Troops in Uniform * The Gateway Pundit * by Cassandra MacDonald
sources.text:
Navy and Marine Corps separation boards are repeatedly voting to keep transgender service members despite Pentagon rules that leave them almost no choice but to recommend discharge, according to a new report.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the policy in blunt terms during a September “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico.
“No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals,” Hegseth told the audience, describing the people he said had no place in the military under the Trump administration’s push for higher standards and the end of woke ideology.
.@SECWAR “It’s worth saying again so that the fake news understands it.
We are no longer the woke department or the weak department… no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdoes, no wimps, no radicals—JUST WARRIORS.” https://t.co/6pGxRUK47r
— DOW Rapid Response (@DOWResponse) September 30, 2026
The boards were created to process remaining cases after President Donald Trump’s executive order and Hegseth’s guidance barred service by those with “gender dysphoria” or related treatments.
Many of the roughly 4,200 openly transgender troops identified by the Pentagon accepted separation payments and left, but some stayed and demanded the peer-review process.
The boards, staffed by everyday uniformed personnel and given instructions that any evidence of transgender status requires dismissal regardless of performance, have not followed orders in most Navy and Marine cases.
The New York Times found these boards voted to retain the member in nine of 12 proceedings.
Outsiders, including spouses, are barred from the proceedings, and the Pentagon has not released official tallies.
The figures came from interviews with participants and lawyers.
New York Times military correspondent Dave Philipps described the process to CNN.
“So what’s interesting is these boards are set up sort of like jury duty to pull every day Marines and sailors and have them apply the rules, and kick trans service members out. And these rules are written so narrowly that they’re really left with no choice,” he said.
“If anyone has any sign of being transgender, even if they’re a decorated war hero or a really needed highly-trained technician, the juries have no leeway. If transgender, then you must throw them out. But that’s not what these boards are doing.”
Philipps continued, “All of a sudden, they are looking at these rules, realizing that they’re given no choice, and then they’ve been voting over and over — about three out of every four times — to keep these transgender soldiers and sailors and Marines in uniform, which is basically them quietly defying orders.”
“I think what the boards are doing is saying, ‘Look, we’re being presented with someone who is good at their job, has never broken any rules, and in some cases, is a highly-valued member of the military. And we’re being told to throw them out,’ and they’re just saying, ‘No.’ In fact, in some cases, in the Marine Corps, I saw paperwork where they actually scratched out the instructions on their paperwork that said, ‘You must discharge this person.’ And instead they just voted to keep them.”
Those votes are only recommendations. Branch secretaries appointed by the administration review them and can reverse the outcome.
Philipps noted the pattern is not uniform.
Trending: TRAGIC VIDEO: Man Jumps to His Death from Dallas Highway Bridge After Hours-Long SWAT Standoff — Police Unable to Save Him as Horrified Officers Look On
The Army, the first service to begin hearings, initially discharged nearly everyone, around 95 percent or higher, though more retention recommendations have appeared later.
Air Force boards have “overwhelmingly” voted for separation in the known cases reviewed so far.
One retained Marine, Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras, a supply and logistics specialist with three overseas deployments and a decade of service, told the Times that board members were simply “war fighters looking at war fighters.”
“I was shocked at first, but when you come down to it, it makes sense,” Sergeant Contreras told the NYT. “You have war fighters looking at war fighters,” he said. “They see I’ve always done my job, I’ve deployed, I’ve mentored other Marines, followed the rules. They say, ‘Hey, this is a good Marine, why wouldn’t we retain him?’”
The administration has already limited the boards’ independence. An October 2025 Pentagon memo obtained by the Associated Press allows commanders to override a board’s recommendation to retain a transgender member, breaking with longstanding practice that boards act independently.
Service members appearing before boards have also been required to meet uniform and grooming standards corresponding to their sex assigned at birth, and refusal can be held against them.
About a quarter of the identified transgender troops took voluntary separation payments rather than face the process.
Legal challenges to the transgender troop ban continue, but the Supreme Court has allowed it to remain in effect while litigation proceeds.

sources.news_title: The military’s quiet rebellion against Trump’s anti-trans orders
sources.text:
The Trump administration is facing an unexpected obstacle in its crusade to segregate the military and kick out transgender troops who have signed up to defend their country—and that obstacle is the armed services themselves.
The New York Times reports that review boards set up to execute President Donald Trump’s orders to consider the cases of transgender troops before ultimately removing them are, in at least two branches of the armed services, not giving the administration the rubber stamp it anticipated.
In 12 cases that have come before the Navy and the Marines, boards have voted to retain troops nine times. The Trump purge has been more successful in the Air Force and Army, where troops are more likely to be removed.
Former Air Force lawyer Rachel VanLandingham explained the quiet rebellion to the Times, “We are seeing them nullify a process they see as unjust.”
Marine Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras, who was singled out by the administration for removal but whose review board determined he “remains qualified,” explained the mindset of his fellow servicemembers to the outlet.
“They see I’ve always done my job, I’ve deployed, I’ve mentored other Marines, followed the rules. They say, ‘Hey, this is a good Marine, why wouldn’t we retain him?’” he said.
Contreras’ statement underlines the destructive stance of the administration. If the American military wants to continue to be the most powerful fighting force in the world—fulfilling Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s endless ranting about retaining “war fighters”—shouldn’t able and willing transgender servicemembers be a key part of the equation?
The decision by these review boards to defy Hegseth and Trump is in line with earlier reporting that for all the public bravado expressed by the two Republicans, rank-and-file members of the military do not have respect for the men and their dictates.
To be sure, the boards’ findings can be overruled by political appointees, but the sheer act of quiet defiance undermines years of conservative rhetoric purporting that the movement has the unified support of the armed services.
While attempting to root out transgender service members, Hegseth has also acted to block promotions that were slated to occur for Black and female officers. The former Fox News host who once bragged that he never washes his hands has even put in rules about beard length and shaving that would disproportionately single out Black soldiers for removal.
In a time of peace, the right wing’s push to turn the military into something resembling a conservative safe space consisting of only straight white men (with appropriate testosterone levels) might still be controversial, but Hegseth’s ideas are being implemented while America is stuck in yet another war in the Middle East, with no end in sight.
If battlefield triumph is the end goal—and that’s the entire point of having such a well-financed military—you wouldn’t undermine the fighting force by drumming out the best and the brightest.
But that is precisely what Trump and Hegseth are trying to do, and some of the troops seem to have had enough.

sources.news_title: Pete Hegseth wants trans troops gone. U.S. Navy & USMC review boards keep finding reasons to keep them
sources.text:
The Pentagon wants transgender troops out. Some military officers reviewing their cases have concluded they should stay.
Navy and Marine Corps separation boards have voted to retain transgender service members in nine of 12 cases, The New York Times reported Friday, revealing resistance within the administrative machinery carrying out President Donald Trump’s military ban. Officers reviewing individual service records are reaching conclusions that conflict with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s blanket campaign to remove them.
A favorable vote does not guarantee a future in uniform. But the decisions expose a tension at the center of the policy. The administration says transgender service is incompatible with military readiness; some officers evaluating those troops want to keep them.
Related: Decorated transgender troops endure closed-door hearings with foregone conclusions in Pentagon purge
Marine Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras received one of those votes. According to The Times, his board reviewed his record as a supply and logistics specialist, including three overseas deployments, and recommended retaining him.
“You have war fighters looking at war fighters,” Contreras told the newspaper.
The outcomes differ sharply across the services. The Times reported that Army boards overwhelmingly recommended discharge, while Air Force boards did so in every known case reviewed.
Related: Trans service members have always been part of U.S. history
The Pentagon narrowed the path to staying
The decisions follow the Pentagon’s move to restrict the boards' independence in hearing these cases.
The Associated Press reported last year that an October 2025 memorandum allowed commanders to override board decisions permitting transgender troops to remain. An earlier Air Force directive required boards to recommend separation for service members diagnosed with gender dysphoria.
The Pentagon also required transgender troops appearing before boards to comply with uniform and grooming standards corresponding to their sex assigned at birth. Proceedings could continue without those who refused, and their noncompliance with the humiliation of essentially showing up in drag could be considered against them.
Those rules placed additional obstacles before troops seeking to defend their careers, even when their performance was not in dispute.
Related: Pentagon’s so-called waiver for trans troops is a cruel hoax
In August, Army Capt. Kai Proce’s lawyer presented extensive documentation of his service, awards, and character. Proce had served for 11 years and mentored cadets at West Point. A panel nevertheless voted to remove him based on his gender dysphoria diagnosis and gender-affirming care.
The administration defends the restrictions by citing readiness, deployability, unit cohesion, discipline, and costs. Its lawyers maintain that the policy addresses a medical condition and related treatment rather than transgender identity.
Yet Hegseth has repeatedly described the objective as excluding transgender people, often using anti-trans slurs in speeches and public statements. The Advocate reported this month that Justice Department attorneys asked a federal judge to disregard his social media statements when assessing the policy.
Related: The Trump administration is paying trans troops not to work
A hearing, and an uncertain future
The removal effort also extends to troops identified through their health records. In September, officials were searching medical and personnel data to identify transgender service members.
Meanwhile, troops challenging the ban in court are confronting separation proceedings themselves.
Army Reserve 2nd Lt. Nicolas Talbott, who is suing the Trump administration to serve, told The Advocate this month that he drove nearly two hours to his Ohio unit to receive paperwork initiating his removal. A close friend he worked with handed him the documents.
“I am absolutely invoking my right to a board of inquiry,” Talbott said.
Another plaintiff, Navy Lt. Clara Winchell, appeared before a board in September. It found her disqualified under the policy but recognized that her record otherwise warranted retention. The board recommended postponing her separation pending the litigation.
An appeals court ruled in June in favor of protections for currently serving plaintiffs. But the mandate implementing that ruling remained unissued while the administration pursued Supreme Court review.
Trial is scheduled for January 4.

sources.text:
Posted Zero Hedge
Military boards set up to push transgender troops out of the service are instead voting to keep many of them, the New York Times reported Friday, in a quiet break with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's ban.
Nine of the 12 service members who have come before the boards have been approved to stay, according to the Times. Boards at Marine Corps Base Quantico, assigned to carry out the removals, "were doing the opposite," the paper said, and Navy boards given strict instructions to force out sailors were "voting to let them stay." A Marine staff sergeant who appeared in August thought his career was over, and the panel approved him.
The Air Force is the exception. The Times found no similar pattern there, where transgender airmen are being discharged quickly. The Pentagon has not said how many hearings have been held or how many people have been removed, and the proceedings are closed, even to spouses.
Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force lawyer now at Southwestern Law School, told the Times the boards "are being told to do something that they know is wrong."
The boards are the last step in a removal campaign that began with a January 2025 executive order. In a September 2025 speech at Quantico, Hegseth told troops, "No more identity months, DEI offices, dudes in dresses." The Supreme Court let the ban take effect on May 6, 2025, and Hegseth's May 8 memo gave active-duty troops until June 6 and reservists until July 7 to leave voluntarily before involuntary separation began. Pentagon data from December 2024 counted about 4,240 service members with a gender dysphoria diagnosis.
The boards were designed to reach one result. Priya Rashid, a military attorney who represents transgender service members, told NPR in February that the outcome is "generally predetermined" and put the cost of assembling each board at $22,000.
An October 2025 Pentagon memo lets commanders overturn a board's decision to let a transgender service member stay. The memo, from Undersecretary Anthony Tata and obtained by AP, breaks with longstanding policy that boards act independently. It also requires transgender troops to appear in uniforms matching their birth sex, and a hearing proceeds without them if they refuse.

sources.news_title: Rank-and-file military members are rejecting trans expulsion orders: “Not going to play that game”
sources.text:
Review boards tasked with expelling trans troops from the U.S. military aren’t performing as expected.
The boards, composed of everyday uniformed service members, are voting to keep their trans colleagues.
          
Related
It’s a remarkable rebuke up the chain of command to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who has vilified trans service members as part of a “woke” cadre of “fatties,” “tr***ies,” “beardos,” and “weirdos” infiltrating the military.
Navy and Marine Corps boards have voted to retain trans members in nine of 12 cases since their hearings started in July. The Army rejected expulsion in five cases among several dozen it has heard since February. Only the Air Force panels have voted to expel all trans service members in the six cases it has heard since meetings started over the summer.
    Never Miss a Beat
Subscribe to our newsletter to stay ahead of the latest LGBTQ+ political news and insights.
“These boards are being told to do something that they know is wrong – to rubber-stamp a non-choice given to them by the administration,” Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force lawyer and a professor at Southwestern Law School, told The New York Times.
“We are seeing them say they’re not going to play that game. We are seeing them nullify a process they see as unjust.”
VanLandingham has been tracking the expulsion cases in the absence of any information provided by the Pentagon – speaking to lawyers, service members called up from their regular duties to serve as jurors, and the trans service members who’ve been put before them.
The three-member “separation” boards were created to provide a veneer of due process in Hegseth and President Donald Trump’s crusade against transgender officers and troops in the military, a reboot of the same effort in Trump’s first term. Under the rules, any evidence of a service member being transgender requires dismissal.
The current ban is being litigated, but the Supreme Court allowed it to take effect as challenges make their way through lower courts.
In the meantime, trans service members who did not retire ahead of a deadline last spring are on paid leave and await their hearings and the chance to dispute their expulsion, however unlikely a favorable outcome might be.
Or so they thought.
“I was shocked at first,” Marine Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras said of his hearing in August.
Following a government lawyer’s presentation of documents showing that Contreras transitioned in 2017, the board members reviewed his record, which included three overseas deployments and a decade of flawless service as a supply and logistics specialist.
The Marines then crossed out instructions regarding “a history of cross sex hormone therapy” and circled “remains qualified.” They voted to retain him.
“When you come down to it, it makes sense,” Contreras said. “You have war fighters looking at war fighters. They see I’ve always done my job, I’ve deployed, I’ve mentored other Marines, followed the rules. They say, ‘Hey, this is a good Marine, why wouldn’t we retain him?’”
While his Marine colleagues would, the board decisions are only recommendations. They could be reversed by the like-minded secretaries with whom Hegseth has stocked the service branches.
And scores of trans service members have been expelled in the Pentagon’s trans purge as planned.
Maj. Kara Corcoran, an infantry officer who served for 18 years and deployed to Afghanistan twice, was expelled in May. She called the Army board that heard her case a “kangaroo court.”
“They cut off my character witnesses halfway through and said, ‘We get it, your service is commendable, that’s not what we’re here to decide,’” she said. “The government lawyer, the board, they thought it was ridiculous, but I think they felt they had no choice.”

The sailor, who had received two merit-based promotions and served alongside Marines deployed to the southern border, said all three board members described personally knowing transgender individuals, including former colleagues and friends.
“I never ran into people who cared if I was trans,” the sailor said. “They just cared that I did my job well.”
His attorney, Steph Kral, subsequently represented another sailor before a different board, which also recommended retention despite its members reportedly lacking similar personal connections to transgender service members.
“I don’t think they are trying to make any grand policy statement,” Kral said. “I think they’re just trying to do what’s best for the Navy.”
The report also referenced Hegseth’s September address at Quantico, during which he called for military standards that included “No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals.”
VanLandingham suggested that dissatisfaction with Pentagon leadership could be influencing the boards’ decisions, while Rashid pointed to the Marine Corps’ emphasis on loyalty to fellow Marines.

Lauren Boebert (R-CO) that would have codified Trump’s executive order banning transgender-identifying individuals from military service. sources.news_title: Navy, Marine Corps Boards Defy Orders, Vote To Keep Transgender-Identifying Troops: Report
sources.text:
A week after beginning his second term, President Donald Trump signed an executive order barring transgender-identifying individuals from military service. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has implemented the administration’s ban, including through review boards handling cases involving transgender troops facing discharge.
But some Navy and Marine Corps boards have voted to retain transgender-identifying service members despite instructions aimed at removing them, according to a report by The New York Times.
“Instead of firing trans Marines, the boards were voting to keep them,” the Times wrote, reporting a similar pattern in the Navy.
According to the report, boards from both services have voted to keep transgender-identifying service members in nine of 12 cases identified by the Times. The outlet said its findings came through interviews with service members and lawyers involved, because officials have not released the outcomes.

The proceedings, the Times noted, are conducted in secret, and outsiders, including spouses, are not allowed to attend. The three-person panels are made up of officers and enlisted personnel temporarily assigned from their other jobs to hear a single case, like civilian jurors, according to the outlet.
But the boards’ votes are recommendations, not necessarily final decisions. The secretaries overseeing the military branches can reverse them.
Last year, the Pentagon offered payments to transgender-identifying individuals who voluntarily left the military, while others remained to challenge their dismissals. The administration directed review boards to process the remaining cases under strict instructions, the outlet said. “Under the rules, any evidence of transgender feelings or tendencies — even if there is no formal transition — requires dismissal.”
The Times said it has not so far found a similar pattern in the Army or the Air Force, where boards have overwhelmingly voted to discharge transgender-identifying service members.

sources.news_title: Military Boards Are Defying Hegseth’s Orders To Ban Transgender Troops
Military boards have been quietly defying Trump’s orders
sources.text:
A new report revealed that military members are quietly defying orders from President Donald Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.
Democrats came under fire when former military and intelligence members who are in elected office filmed a video saying that no one in the military must follow an unlawful order. The video reminded anyone in the military that the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) says all military members have a legal right and obligation to refuse unlawful orders.
Trump called it an act of "sedition" and demanded that the members of the legislature be "put on trial." Nov. 20 marks the one-year anniversary of Trump's demand. It hasn't happened. The Defense Department tried to demote Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) so he wouldn't get as much money in his pension.
Now it appears that others have similarly decided to defy orders behind closed doors.
"The Pentagon had set up review boards at bases around the globe, manned by everyday uniformed service members with narrow orders that all but ensured that the trans troops appearing before them would be voted out," said the New York Times on Friday.
But a unique thing is happening: those soldiers on the boards are voting to keep transgender members in the military. The same is happening in the Navy as well.
The report said it isn't happening on occasion; nine of the 12 people brought before the boards have been approved to stay. All of the proceedings are being kept secret and even spouses are prohibited from attending the hearings. The Pentagon won't say how many there have been total or how many people have been removed.
The same move is not happening in the U.S. Air Force, however, where trans military personnel are being discharged quickly. But the Times calls it a "stunning rebuke" of Trumpism by at least some military branches.
“These boards are being told to do something that they know is wrong — to rubber-stamp a non-choice given to them by the administration,” said former Air Force lawyer Rachel VanLandingham, who now teaches at Southwestern Law School. “We are seeing them say they’re not going to play that game. We are seeing them nullify a process they see as unjust.”
"The Trump administration claims that trans troops, who account for about 4,250 people or about 0.1 percent of the military, are a costly burden on military effectiveness," the report said. But it cited a military finding that contradicts that assessment.
“For the sake of our Nation and the patriotic Americans who volunteer to serve it, military service must be reserved for those mentally and physically fit for duty,” the order demands.
The result was significant, the report said.
"Hundreds of highly qualified people left, including doctors, lawyers, pilots and nuclear technicians. The troops who stayed to challenge their dismissal waited in limbo, sometimes for more than a year," the Times said.
The report went on to walk through one Marine Staff Sargent who faced the court in August. He thought that his career was over, but the panel approved him. His lawyer was shocked. She'd seen nothing but losses and dismissals at the beginning of these board meetings, but then something shifted, and she has no idea why. The Navy and Marines refuse to cooperate. Then, recently, she won a case with someone for the Army.
For some who have already been dismissed, however, the experience was very different. After 18 years, one woman had a character witness testifying on her behalf when the panel cut them off and said, "We get it, your service is commendable, that’s not what we’re here to decide."

sources.news_title: Hegseth Barred Trans Troops - Yet Navy And Marine Boards Are Voting To Keep Them
sources.text:
Hegseth Barred Trans Troops - Yet Navy And Marine Boards Are Voting To Keep Them
Military boards set up to push transgender troops out of the service are instead voting to keep many of them, the New York Times reported Friday, in a quiet break with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's ban.
Nine of the 12 service members who have come before the boards have been approved to stay, according to the Times. Boards at Marine Corps Base Quantico, assigned to carry out the removals, "were doing the opposite," the paper said, and Navy boards given strict instructions to force out sailors were "voting to let them stay." A Marine staff sergeant who appeared in August thought his career was over, and the panel approved him.
The Air Force is the exception. The Times found no similar pattern there, where transgender airmen are being discharged quickly. The Pentagon has not said how many hearings have been held or how many people have been removed, and the proceedings are closed, even to spouses.
Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force lawyer now at Southwestern Law School, told the Times the boards "are being told to do something that they know is wrong."
The boards are the last step in a removal campaign that began with a January 2025 executive order. In a September 2025 speech at Quantico, Hegseth told troops, "No more identity months, DEI offices, dudes in dresses." The Supreme Court let the ban take effect on May 6, 2025, and Hegseth's May 8 memo gave active-duty troops until June 6 and reservists until July 7 to leave voluntarily before involuntary separation began. Pentagon data from December 2024 counted about 4,240 service members with a gender dysphoria diagnosis.
The boards were designed to reach one result. Priya Rashid, a military attorney who represents transgender service members, told NPR in February that the outcome is "generally predetermined" and put the cost of assembling each board at $22,000.
An October 2025 Pentagon memo lets commanders overturn a board's decision to let a transgender service member stay. The memo, from Undersecretary Anthony Tata and obtained by AP, breaks with longstanding policy that boards act independently. It also requires transgender troops to appear in uniforms matching their birth sex, and a hearing proceeds without them if they refuse.

sources.news_title: Military Boards Are Quietly Defying Hegseth’s Transgender Ban Orders by Voting to Keep Gender-Confused Troops in Uniform
sources.text:
Image: Wikimedia Commons (DOD photo by U.S. Air Force Senior Airman Madelyn Keech) Navy and Marine Corps separation boards are repeatedly ...
Navy and Marine Corps separation boards are repeatedly voting to keep transgender service members despite Pentagon rules that leave them almost no choice but to recommend discharge, according to a new report.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the policy in blunt terms during a September “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico.
“No fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals,” Hegseth told the audience, describing the people he said had no place in the military under the Trump administration’s push for higher standards and the end of woke ideology.
The boards were created to process remaining cases after President Donald Trump’s executive order and Hegseth’s guidance barred service by those with “gender dysphoria” or related treatments.
Many of the roughly 4,200 openly transgender troops identified by the Pentagon accepted separation payments and left, but some stayed and demanded the peer-review process.
The boards, staffed by everyday uniformed personnel and given instructions that any evidence of transgender status requires dismissal regardless of performance, have not followed orders in most Navy and Marine cases.
The New York Times found these boards voted to retain the member in nine of 12 proceedings.
Outsiders, including spouses, are barred from the proceedings, and the Pentagon has not released official tallies.
The figures came from interviews with participants and lawyers.
New York Times military correspondent Dave Philipps described the process to CNN.
“So what’s interesting is these boards are set up sort of like jury duty to pull every day Marines and sailors and have them apply the rules, and kick trans service members out. And these rules are written so narrowly that they’re really left with no choice,” he said.
“If anyone has any sign of being transgender, even if they’re a decorated war hero or a really needed highly-trained technician, the juries have no leeway. If transgender, then you must throw them out. But that’s not what these boards are doing.”
Philipps continued, “All of a sudden, they are looking at these rules, realizing that they’re given no choice, and then they’ve been voting over and over — about three out of every four times — to keep these transgender soldiers and sailors and Marines in uniform, which is basically them quietly defying orders.”
“I think what the boards are doing is saying, ‘Look, we’re being presented with someone who is good at their job, has never broken any rules, and in some cases, is a highly-valued member of the military. And we’re being told to throw them out,’ and they’re just saying, ‘No.’ In fact, in some cases, in the Marine Corps, I saw paperwork where they actually scratched out the instructions on their paperwork that said, ‘You must discharge this person.’ And instead they just voted to keep them.”
Those votes are only recommendations. Branch secretaries appointed by the administration review them and can reverse the outcome.
Philipps noted the pattern is not uniform.
The Army, the first service to begin hearings, initially discharged nearly everyone, around 95 percent or higher, though more retention recommendations have appeared later.
Air Force boards have “overwhelmingly” voted for separation in the known cases reviewed so far.
One retained Marine, Staff Sgt. Damien Contreras, a supply and logistics specialist with three overseas deployments and a decade of service, told the Times that board members were simply “war fighters looking at war fighters.”
“I was shocked at first, but when you come down to it, it makes sense,” Sergeant Contreras told the NYT. “You have war fighters looking at war fighters,” he said. “They see I’ve always done my job, I’ve deployed, I’ve mentored other Marines, followed the rules. They say, ‘Hey, this is a good Marine, why wouldn’t we retain him?’”
The administration has already limited the boards’ independence. An October 2025 Pentagon memo obtained by the Associated Press allows commanders to override a board’s recommendation to retain a transgender member, breaking with longstanding practice that boards act independently.
Service members appearing before boards have also been required to meet uniform and grooming standards corresponding to their sex assigned at birth, and refusal can be held against them.
About a quarter of the identified transgender troops took voluntary separation payments rather than face the process.
Legal challenges to the transgender troop ban continue, but the Supreme Court has allowed it to remain in effect while litigation proceeds.
